annotation.title_clean: Robot taxation as a fiscal policy instrument for sustainable employment: A scoping review with implications for developing economies
annotation.title_en: Robot taxation as a fiscal policy instrument for sustainable employment: A scoping review with implications for developing economies
named_instruments_referenced: EU Civil Law Rules on Robotics 2017
annotation.summary_en: Scoping review (Arksey and O'Malley) of the literature on robot taxation, focused on South Africa. It argues that automation erodes income tax revenue and that a robot tax could offset the losses, fund worker retraining, and correct tax biases favouring capital over labour.
key_provisions_or_claims: Automation reduces employment-based income tax revenue and widens inequality.
Tax systems such as South Africa's favour capital over labour through generous deductions for machinery.
A robot tax could offset lost revenue and fund retraining and reskilling.
Practical challenges include defining a robot, identifying the taxpayer, and international tax competition.
Oberson's imputed-salary model and international coordination are discussed as design options.
